claims.text: Ghurni, a neighbourhood of Krishnanagar in Nadia district, West Bengal, is the centre for the production of clay dolls often called Krishnanagar clay dolls.

claims.text: The famous clay models of Krishnanagar originate in Ghurni, whose clay model artists have won international repute for their excellence in clay modelling.

quotes.quote: The origin of famous clay models of Krishnanagar is Ghurni. The clay model artists of Ghurni have won international repute and fame for their excellence in clay modelling.

claims.text: Ghurni's clay dolls are famed for realistic depictions of everyday village life, such as farming, rag picking, basket making, cooking and worshipping.

the prime source of entertainment for children used to be these clay dolls, which we also know as 'matir putul.'

lede.text: Ghurni, a neighbourhood of Krishnanagar in Nadia district, West Bengal, is the centre for the production of clay dolls often called Krishnanagar clay dolls.
The dolls are famed for realistic depictions of everyday village life, and the doll makers also make life-like models of eminent personalities and idols of deities.
In 1728 Maharaja Krishnachandra brought potters to Krishnanagar from Dacca and Natore, and doll making at Ghurni gained momentum under his patronage.
The Pal families are inseparable from the history of the clay dolls of Krishnanagar, a Deccan Herald feature says.

sentences.text: In 1728 Maharaja Krishnachandra brought potters to Krishnanagar from Dacca and Natore, and doll making at Ghurni gained momentum under his patronage.
A Deccan Herald feature and Das both put the craft's age at about 250 years, though Das also writes that the community has practised since the 19th century.

The 1978 Nadia gazetteer calls Ghurni famous for several centuries for the manufacture of clay figures, and Mukharji wrote in 1888 that the Krishnagar modelling industry originated from the making of idols for worship.

The British patronised the art and took the dolls to various exhibitions, and Mukharji wrote in 1888 that Krishnagar's modellers had repeatedly gained medals and certificates at most International Exhibitions held since 1851.
Exhibitions of the models were held in London, Paris and Boston, and the artisans earned laurels from British royalty such as Queen Victoria.
In the 19th century, small clay figurines were produced in Indian cities including Krishnagar and sold to visiting Europeans.
Sri Ram Paul (1819-1885) was the first rewarded artist, and Kartik Chandra Pal's statues of Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore found pride of place in Washington DC and Moscow.
The petering out of the zamindari-babu culture brought a continuous erosion of patronage for the clay modellers.
Doll making starts with preparing the clay: the soil is cleared of pebbles and stones, made into a dough by hand and left for at least one night to make it ready for the mould.
The body is made by hand, sometimes on a frame of iron wires or bamboo pieces, and its features, hands, hair and feet are defined with clay modelling tools.
Next the models are dried, usually in the open under sunlight and sometimes with a hand blower.

Sources differ on hardening: the fully dried dolls are placed in a furnace for 4 to 5 hours at 500 degrees centigrade, while Das writes that sun-dried clay dolls have been used since King Krishna Chandra.
After firing the dolls are painted with vibrant colours and decorated with clothes and ornaments, and giving the eyes and facial expressions is the most vital part.
After painting, kerosene is added to the burnish, which increases the brightness of the dolls.
The soil for Ghurni's clay idols and dolls is traditionally collected near the Jalangi River, from whose riverside alluvial soil is available.
The quality of the river soil is being reduced by human interference, and the properties of the silt are inferior for crafting idols.
Das's survey, published in 2026, lists the raw materials for one doll as 300 gram of clay, 10 gram of colour, 5 gram of gum, 10 gram of G.I. wire and 5 gram of cotton.
In 1888 Mukharji recorded real fabric, hair, wool, straw and grass on Krishnagar figures, which gave them a very life-like appearance.
A clay drummer figure in the V&A, probably made in Krishnanagar, is modelled and painted clay with fabric, feather and fibre, the fibre forming its hair and moustache.
Many craftspersons have moved to plaster of Paris work or fibre casting.
The clay doll industry of Krishnanagar is made up mainly of small, family-run firms, and the craftsmen's earnings are seasonal, depending on market demand, festivals and tourists.
A Ghurni artisans' cooperative filed GI application 795, Clay Doll of Krishnanagar, in 2021, and The Statesman reported that the GI Registry had approved it.
The 1978 Nadia gazetteer counted about 175 clay modellers in the Ghurni area, working mostly with the labour of family members.
In Das's survey of Ghurni producers, published in 2026, 42.5% earned less than 3000 rupees a month and only 15% earned above 5000 rupees.
In the same survey, 97.5% of the producers said their profit level had decreased.
In 1978 the gazetteer reported younger people taking up other trades for a better livelihood, and Das writes that present generations tend towards higher education and service-sector jobs.
One study reports that Ghurni exports models of clay, terracotta, fibre and glass, cement, stone and bronze to America, Australia and European countries.
Durable plastic and fibre-cast products have reduced the demand for traditional clay dolls and pottery.
Krishnanagar clay models reproduce the social scenes of the country and its people, its castes and racial types, realistically.
Social scenes such as a collector's court, a tea garden, a pandit-sabha and the Charak festival are used as subjects for modelling.
Popular models include the Baul couple, the farmer, the blacksmith, the tribal couple and the Jhulan doll.
Detailing of form, feature and stance, realism of the clothes to the last fold and tuck, and marvellous expressions make each doll a collector's item.
Mukherjee's Art Manufactures of India describes such realistic models as a feature of the model makers at Krishnagar, a town near Calcutta.
Krishnanagar, the headquarters of Nadia district, stands on the bank of the Jalangi River, though a Telegraph travel feature names the river Churni.
The Ghurni artisan community spreads over the colonies of Pal Para, Halder Para, Sandhya Para, Kalipur, Bhatjangla and Rathtala.
The community's primary water source is the Jalangi River, with local ponds, tube wells and wells available nearby.
Easily available water from the Jalangi River and its alluvial soil helped the clay doll industry flourish at Ghurni, Sanyal and Chaudhuri write.
